This is goal g-33a7a4ae, round 2 (fix round; round 1 was audit-only and already merged as docs/state/silent-failures.md; several fix batches already merged for other files). Read that doc's methodology section first (top of file) and the per-file section for tools/concurrency-guard.mjs (search for '### tools/concurrency-guard.mjs' - it lists exact line numbers and the catch form found there, all try-catch-no-binding).

IMPORTANT - this file is sensitive: it implements `swarm with-concurrency N -- COMMAND`, which spawns a wrapped child process and a watcher process, and kills them (SIGTERM then SIGKILL) on normal exit, a crash of the wrapper itself, Ctrl-C, or a leftover marker from a prior power cut. Six of the eight flagged catches (re-find them by content, not by exact line number) wrap `process.kill(...)` calls in exactly this kill-cleanup logic. The expected case there is the process already being gone (ESRCH) - `kill` on an already-dead pid throws, and that's normal, not a bug. Your fix must, for every one of those process.kill catches: (a) keep the kill call itself completely unchanged (same target, same signal, same timing, same surrounding wait-loop logic), (b) keep the cleanup non-blocking and never add a throw that could stop a restore (this tool's whole job is making sure machineConcurrency config always gets put back), (c) narrow the catch to stay silent for the expected ESRCH case and log anything else unexpected via console.error.

The other two flagged catches (noteChild's marker write, and the config-restore in the signal-handler finish() function) are NOT process-kill related - they are best-effort config/marker bookkeeping. Treat those as ordinary best-effort fallbacks per the rules below (narrow to ENOENT where it applies, log anything else).

For EACH flagged line in tools/concurrency-guard.mjs only (do not touch any other file, do not touch anything beyond the flagged catch blocks, do not touch the restore()/apply() functions' own logic or the signal-handling control flow):

1. Read the surrounding function to understand what the catch is actually guarding against and what happens today when it swallows silently (what does the function return/do next).
2. Decide, from the real code, whether this catch is:
   (a) An EXPECTED/benign condition - the process-already-gone case described above for the six kill sites, or a best-effort marker/config read/write for the other two. For these, keep the swallow (do not change control flow or add noisy logging for the expected path), but narrow to the specific expected error code (ESRCH for kill calls, ENOENT where a marker/config file may not exist) and add minimal visibility (see point 3) for anything else unexpected - same return value, same behavior, just visible.
   (b) A genuinely UNEXPECTED-error catch with no narrower expected case. Add minimal visibility only: a one-line log. This file has no existing logger/journal convention of its own - use `console.error('[tools/concurrency-guard.mjs] <short context naming the function/operation>:', error?.message ?? error)`. Do NOT add a throw, do NOT change the function's return value or control flow, do NOT change what happens next.
3. If a catch binds no error variable, add a REAL binding and actually reference it in a console.error call - do not just rename-and-ignore a binding (including via a `void error;` no-op).

Do not refactor anything beyond the flagged catch blocks. Do not reformat unrelated code. Do not rename functions or change exports. Preserve every existing behavior path exactly except for the narrowing/visibility described above.

Your workspace does not include the test suite, so you cannot run it yourself - the orchestrator runs the real full suite against your output after integration, and will also get this reviewed by Opus before merge given the sensitivity (process-kill), and will send back any issue as a follow-up. List, in your final summary, which of the 8 flagged lines you touched, case (a) vs (b), with one line each, and confirm the kill()/apply()/restore() calls themselves are unchanged.
